title: Who Is This? The Christ, the Cross, and the Road to Jerusalem
summary: Jesus sends out the Twelve, Herod wonders who he is, and Jesus feeds five thousand people from five loaves and two fish. Peter confesses him as the Christ of God, and Jesus begins to teach that the Son of Man must suffer and that followers must take up their cross daily. On a mountain he is transfigured before three disciples; afterward he heals a boy, rebukes the disciples' ambitions, and sets his face toward Jerusalem, warning would-be followers of the cost.
story:
This chapter is the hinge of Luke's Gospel. The question that has been building since chapter 5 (“Who is this?”, 5:21, 7:49, 8:25) is asked by Herod (verse 9), answered by Peter (verse 20), and confirmed by the Father's voice on the mountain (verse 35). Once Jesus' identity is confessed, he reveals his destiny: rejection, death, and resurrection. The disciples, who have just been given power to heal and proclaim, prove in the chapter's second half that they do not yet understand: they cannot heal a boy, they do not grasp the passion prediction, they argue about greatness, they try to stop an outsider, and they want to call down fire on a village.

Then, at verse 51, Luke begins a long section, running to about 19:27 or 19:44, in which Jesus travels toward Jerusalem, where that destiny waits. It is often called the travel narrative or central section. Much of Jesus' best-known teaching in Luke, including the Good Samaritan, the lost sheep, coin, and son, and the rich man and Lazarus, is set along this road, and most of it is found only in Luke. The Galilean ministry closes; the road to the cross opens.
historical:
Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. Tetrarch, literally ruler of a fourth part, had come to mean a minor ruler under Rome. Antipas had John beheaded; Mark 6:14-29 tells that story at length, while Luke reports only Herod's own words, “I beheaded John” (verse 9). Josephus gives a political motive for the execution, Antipas's fear that John's influence over the crowds might lead to revolt, and places it at the fortress of Machaerus (Antiquities 18.116-119). Antipas's anxious curiosity (verse 9) is paid off later, when he finally sees Jesus at his trial and hopes for a miracle (23:8-12).

Bethsaida (verse 10), ‘house of fishing’, lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee on the northeast, in the territory of Herod Philip, another son of Herod the Great. Josephus says Philip raised the village to the rank of a city and named it Julias after the emperor's daughter Julia (Antiquities 18.28). Its site is disputed. Rami Arav's excavations at et-Tell, begun in 1987, long made it the leading candidate, while since 2016 Mordechai Aviam and R. Steven Notley have excavated el-Araj, nearer the shore, and argue that its Roman-period remains fit Josephus's Julias better. The feeding itself took place in a deserted place near the town (verse 12).

Between the feeding (Mark 6:30-44) and Peter's confession (Mark 8:27-30), Mark includes a long stretch of material (Mark 6:45-8:26: walking on the water, disputes over purity, the Syrophoenician woman, a second feeding, and more) that Luke leaves out entirely. Scholars call this Luke's great omission. Whether Luke's copy of Mark lacked the section or he chose to omit it is debated; the effect is to bring the feeding and the confession close together. Luke also omits the place of the confession, Caesarea Philippi (Mark 8:27), and sets it instead in a moment of Jesus' prayer (verse 18).

The Samaritans (verse 52) lived in the hill country between Galilee and Judea. They traced their descent to the old northern tribes of Israel, accepted only the five books of Moses as Scripture, and worshiped on Mount Gerizim near Shechem rather than in Jerusalem. Jews often viewed them through 2 Kings 17:24-41, as descendants of peoples the Assyrians settled in the land after 722 BC, while Samaritans regarded themselves as the faithful remnant of Israel. The Hasmonean ruler John Hyrcanus destroyed their sanctuary on Gerizim (Josephus, Antiquities 13.254-256); coins from the excavations there by Yitzhak Magen point to about 111 or 110 BC. Hostility ran deep on both sides. Josephus reports that some Samaritans scattered human bones in the Jerusalem temple at Passover during the governorship of Coponius, about AD 6 to 9 (Antiquities 18.29-30), and that around AD 51 or 52 Galilean pilgrims passing through Samaria to a festival were attacked and killed at a village called Ginae, which led to reprisals and an inquiry under the governor Cumanus (Antiquities 20.118-136, Jewish War 2.232-246). Galileans going to Jerusalem could take the direct road through Samaria, a trip of about three days, or go around by the Jordan valley. The village's refusal “because He was heading for Jerusalem” (verse 53) belongs to that history.

Crucifixion was the Roman punishment for rebels, bandits, and slaves, meant to shame as well as kill. Condemned men carried their own crossbeams to the place of execution; Plutarch, writing about AD 100, uses the image of each criminal carrying his own cross as a figure for wickedness bearing its own punishment (On the Delays of Divine Vengeance 554A-B). In 1968 an ossuary found at Giv'at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem held the heel bone of a first-century crucified man named Yehohanan, with an iron nail still through it, physical evidence of the practice in Jesus' time and place.
cultural:
The Twelve were to travel with nothing: no staff, no bag, no bread, no money, no second tunic (verse 3), and to depend on the hospitality of those who welcomed them. Wandering Cynic philosophers of the period were known for a staff and a beggar's bag; the disciples are forbidden even those, so their poverty is not a philosophical pose but total dependence on God and on the households that receive them. Gerd Theissen (Soziologie der Jesusbewegung, 1977; in English, Sociology of Early Palestinian Christianity, 1978) described the early Jesus movement as wandering charismatics supported by settled sympathizers, a pattern this chapter shows. Staying in one house (verse 4) avoided the appearance of shopping for better hospitality. Shaking dust from the feet (verse 5) was a public sign of breaking off responsibility, a solemn act Paul and Barnabas perform in Acts 13:51.

In the feeding, the command to seat the crowd in groups of about fifty (verse 14) recalls the ordering of Israel in the wilderness under leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens (Exodus 18:21, 25). The five thousand are men (andres), so the crowd with women and children was larger. The actions of verse 16, taking, looking up to heaven, blessing, breaking, and giving, follow the pattern of a Jewish head of household saying the blessing over bread at a meal, and Luke repeats the same verbs at the Last Supper (22:19) and at Emmaus (24:30). The twelve baskets were probably the wicker baskets travelers carried for food.

Peter's offer to put up three shelters (skēnai, verse 33) recalls the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles, when Israel lived in temporary shelters for seven days to remember the wilderness years (Leviticus 23:42-43), and the tabernacle where God's glory dwelt (Exodus 40:34). The cloud that overshadows them is the cloud of God's presence from Sinai and the tabernacle.

Burying a father was among the most sacred duties of a son in Jewish life. The Mishnah exempts a man whose dead relative lies before him awaiting burial from reciting the Shema and from prayer and tefillin (m. Berakhot 3:1), so pressing was the obligation. Jesus' reply to the man who asks first to bury his father (verses 59-60) is therefore startling. Some suggest that the father was not yet dead and the man meant he would follow after his father's eventual death. Byron McCane (Harvard Theological Review, 1990) proposed a different setting: in the first century Jews often buried a body in a family tomb and, about a year later, gathered the bones into a stone box (ossuary), a duty that fell to the son, so the man may have been asking to wait out the year until the reburial. Either way, Jesus' reply claims a priority higher than the strongest family duty. The last would-be follower's request to say farewell to his family (verse 61) echoes Elisha's request to kiss his father and mother before following Elijah (1 Kings 19:20), which Elijah allowed. A plowman who looks back cuts a crooked furrow; the image asks for undivided attention.
literary:
Luke 9:1-50 is built around the question of Jesus' identity. Herod's question (“who is this man I hear such things about?”, verse 9) and the crowds' opinions (verses 7-8 and 19, John raised, Elijah, one of the old prophets) frame Peter's confession, “The Christ of God” (verse 20). The Father's voice on the mountain gives the fullest answer, “This is My Son, whom I have chosen” (verse 35). The chapter then turns on the passion predictions in verses 22 and 44, the first two of three in Luke (the third is 18:31-33). Each time, glory is followed at once by the cross: the confession by the prediction of suffering, the transfiguration by a failure and a second prediction, the disciples' marveling (verse 43) by the warning that the Son of Man will be delivered into human hands.

The transfiguration echoes Moses on Sinai: a mountain, a changed face (compare Exodus 34:29-35), a cloud, God's voice, and a command to listen, which recalls Moses' promise of a prophet like himself, “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). Luke dates it “about eight days” after the preceding sayings (Mark 9:2 has after six days), and only Luke says that Jesus went up to pray and was transfigured while praying (verses 28-29), that Moses and Elijah spoke of Jesus' departure, using the Greek word exodos (verse 31), and that the disciples were heavy with sleep (verse 32), a detail that anticipates their sleep in Gethsemane (22:45).

The chapter contains several echoes of Elijah. The crowds think Jesus may be Elijah returned (verses 8, 19); Elijah appears on the mountain; the disciples want to call down fire as Elijah did (verse 54, 2 Kings 1:10-12); the word for Jesus' taking up (analēmpsis, verse 51) recalls Elijah being taken up into heaven (2 Kings 2:11), for which the Greek Old Testament uses the related verb; and the would-be follower's request echoes Elisha's (1 Kings 19:20). Jesus is like Elijah and greater than Elijah, and he refuses the fire.

The final section begins with a solemn phrase (verse 51), literally ‘he set his face to go to Jerusalem’, which recalls the resolve of the Servant in Isaiah 50:7 (“I have set My face like flint”) and the prophet told to set his face toward a place in judgment (Ezekiel 21:2). The travel narrative that follows has little geography and much teaching. Hans Conzelmann (Die Mitte der Zeit, 1954, translated as The Theology of St. Luke, 1960) argued that it is a theological construction rather than an itinerary; C. F. Evans (The Central Section of St. Luke's Gospel, 1955) proposed that it follows the order of Deuteronomy, and David Moessner (Lord of the Banquet, 1989) read it as the march of the prophet like Moses toward his exodus. Parallels to the chapter are found in Mark 6:6-44, 8:27-9:41, and Matthew 10, 14, 16, 17, and 8:19-22.

Herod's perplexity
Five thousand fed
Peter's confession and the first passion prediction

The transfiguration
A boy healed and a second passion prediction
Who is the greatest
Setting out for Jerusalem; a Samaritan village refuses
The cost of following

doctrines.note: Peter confesses Jesus as “The Christ of God” (verse 20), and Jesus immediately defines what that means: a Messiah who must suffer, be rejected, be killed, and be raised (verse 22). The title is true, but the popular expectation of it must be remade by the cross. At the crucifixion the rulers will mock him with the same title: “if He is the Christ of God, the Chosen One” (23:35).

The Son of Man must suffer (verse 22). The word must (dei) signals divine necessity: Jesus' death is not an accident of politics but the accomplishment of God's plan, the exodus he will fulfill at Jerusalem (verse 31). Luke does not yet explain how the death saves; he establishes that it is purposed by God and freely embraced.

On the mountain the disciples “saw Jesus’ glory” (verse 32), and Jesus speaks of coming in his glory and the Father's (verse 26). The transfiguration is a preview of the glory that belongs to him and that he will enter through suffering (24:26), given to strengthen disciples who have just heard that he must die.

Jesus gives the Twelve power and authority and sends them to proclaim the kingdom and heal (verses 1-2), the first of Luke's sending scenes, followed by the seventy-two in chapter 10 and the whole church in Acts. Their mission shares his: dependence on God, a message of the kingdom, and the risk of rejection.

Verse 51 names Jesus' goal as his analēmpsis, his taking up. Luke's use of the related verb for the ascension (Acts 1:2, 1:11, 1:22) suggests that the road to Jerusalem leads not only to the cross but through resurrection to Jesus' exaltation to the Father's right hand.

words.note: Exodos, departure, going out, exit. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: here, in Hebrews 11:22 for the exodus of Israel from Egypt, and in 2 Peter 1:15 for Peter's approaching death. In Greek it could mean death, as a euphemism, and the book of Exodus bears it as its title in the Greek tradition. Luke's choice in verse 31 lets both senses sound: Jesus' death, and beyond it his resurrection and ascension, will be a new exodus, God's great act of rescue for his people. The verb with it, plēroō, to fulfill or accomplish, presents the departure as a mission to be completed rather than a fate to be suffered.

Analēmpsis, a taking up. It occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb analambanō is used of Elijah's being taken up into heaven in the Greek Old Testament (2 Kings 2:9-11) and of Jesus' ascension in Acts 1:2, 1:11, and 1:22. Some interpreters take the noun here to mean Jesus' death, as it sometimes can in later Greek; most take it as the whole movement of death, resurrection, and ascension, with the ascension as its end point.

Dei, it is necessary, one must. This impersonal verb occurs about 101 times in the New Testament, 18 of them in Luke and 22 in Acts, more than in any other books. Luke uses it for the divine necessity that governs Jesus' life, from the boy in the temple who must be in his Father's house (2:49) to the risen Christ explaining that everything written about him must be fulfilled (24:7, 24:26, 24:44). In verse 22 it makes the suffering of the Son of Man part of God's plan.

Stauros, cross, the upright stake with or without a crossbeam used by Rome for executions meant to shame. It occurs 27 times in the New Testament. To take up a cross meant to walk toward one's own death under public disgrace. Jesus uses it of discipleship (verse 23) before he carries his own, and Luke alone adds daily (kath' hēmeran), making it the shape of an ordinary life rather than a single heroic moment.

Arneomai, to deny, disown, refuse. It occurs 33 times in the New Testament. In verse 23 the critical text has this simple verb where many manuscripts, like Mark 8:34, have the compound aparneomai. To deny oneself is to refuse the self's claim to be master. The same verb describes Peter's later denial of Jesus (22:57): under pressure, a disciple either says no to the self or says no to Jesus.

Doxa, glory. It occurs about 166 times in the New Testament and 13 in Luke. In ordinary Greek it meant opinion or reputation, but the Greek Old Testament used it for the Hebrew kavod, the weighty, radiant presence of God that filled the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34). Luke uses it three times here: the Son of Man's coming glory (verse 26), Moses and Elijah appearing in glory (verse 31), and Jesus' own glory seen by the disciples (verse 32).

Eklegomai, to choose, select. It occurs 22 times in the New Testament. In verse 35 the perfect passive participle, ho eklelegmenos, the one who has been chosen, gives Luke's form of the heavenly voice, where Mark and Matthew have beloved. It echoes Isaiah 42:1, where God presents “My Servant, whom I uphold, My Chosen One”, and it returns at the cross when the rulers mock “the Christ of God, the Chosen One” (23:35).

Skēnē, tent, booth, tabernacle. It occurs 20 times in the New Testament, ten of them in Hebrews, where it names the wilderness tabernacle. Peter's three skēnai (verse 33) recall the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles and the tent where God's glory dwelt among Israel. His wish to stay on the mountain misunderstands the moment: the glory will not be housed in booths but will go down the mountain and on to Jerusalem.

christ:
Here Jesus is identified by the church's first confession, the Christ of God (verse 20), and by the Father's own words, “This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him!” (verse 35). The voice gathers three strands of Scripture: the royal Son of Psalm 2:7, whom God installs as king; the Chosen One of Isaiah 42:1, the Servant in whom God delights and who will suffer (Isaiah 52:13-53:12); and the prophet like Moses, “You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). The transfiguration gives three disciples a glimpse of the glory that belongs to him, and Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets, talk with him about his exodus. After the resurrection Jesus will say that Moses and all the Prophets spoke of his suffering and glory (24:27, 24:44). On the mountain they do so in person.

The feeding of the five thousand shows him as the one who provides for God's people in a deserted place as God gave manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and as the shepherd-king who feeds the flock (Ezekiel 34:23). His taking, blessing, breaking, and giving anticipate the Last Supper (22:19) and the meal at Emmaus where he is known in the breaking of the bread (24:30-35). The link with the manna is a pattern, not a prediction, but Luke's wording invites the reader to see it.

Yet this glorious Son sets his face toward Jerusalem to be delivered into human hands (verse 44). He is greater than Elijah, but where Elijah called down fire on the king's soldiers (2 Kings 1:10-12), Jesus rebukes the disciples who want to do the same and goes on to another village (verses 55-56); later in Luke, Samaritans become examples of compassion and gratitude (10:33, 17:16), and in Acts the gospel reaches Samaria (Acts 8:5-25). Luke's picture holds glory and suffering together. The way to the glory the disciples glimpsed runs through the cross, and he calls his followers to walk the same road daily.
interpretation:
The transfiguration drew more interpretation than anything else in the chapter. Christian tradition from the third century placed it on Mount Tabor in Galilee: Origen already names Tabor, and Cyril of Jerusalem does so in his Catechetical Lectures (about 350); the present Franciscan basilica on the summit was completed in 1924. Many modern scholars prefer Mount Hermon, nearer Caesarea Philippi, where Mark and Matthew set the preceding confession. Leo the Great (Sermon 51) taught that the chief purpose of the transfiguration was to remove the scandal of the cross from the disciples' hearts by showing them the hidden dignity of the one who would suffer, and to give the church hope that its members would share the glory that shone in its Head. In the East the event became central to the theology of deification. In the fourteenth century Gregory Palamas, in his Triads in Defense of the Holy Hesychasts, defended monks who prayed to see the light of Tabor, arguing that it was the uncreated energy of God and not a created phenomenon, against Barlaam of Calabria; councils at Constantinople between 1341 and 1351 upheld his teaching. The feast of the Transfiguration on August 6 is ancient in the East; in the West Pope Callixtus III made it universal in 1457, in thanksgiving for the lifting of the siege of Belgrade in 1456. Raphael's Transfiguration (1516-1520, now in the Vatican Pinacoteca), his last great painting, sets the radiant Christ above and the disciples' failure with the convulsed boy below, joining verses 28-36 and 37-43 as Luke does.

The call to take up the cross daily (verse 23) shaped Christian spirituality. Thomas à Kempis's Imitation of Christ (about 1420) devotes a chapter to the royal way of the holy cross. Dietrich Bonhoeffer's Discipleship (1937) uses the three would-be followers of verses 57-62 to show how people try to set their own conditions on Jesus' call, which he held must be obeyed at once. The saying about the dead burying their dead has been a test case for historians: Martin Hengel (Nachfolge und Charisma, 1968; in English, The Charismatic Leader and His Followers, 1981) argued that it breaks both law and piety and reveals an authority beyond any rabbi's, and E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) agreed that here, exceptionally, Jesus required disobedience to a commandment of the Torah, while others, such as Byron McCane (1990), read it against burial customs that soften the clash.

The Samaritan village and the disciples' wish for fire mattered in the second-century debate with Marcion, who rejected the God of the Old Testament as a harsh being unlike the Father of Jesus. Marcion contrasted Elijah's fire with Jesus' rebuke; Tertullian (Against Marcion 4.23, around 208) answered that the Creator himself had promised the gentleness of Christ, and that Elijah learned on Horeb that the Lord was not in the fire. The longer text of verses 54-56, in which Jesus tells the disciples they do not know what spirit they are of and that the Son of Man came not to destroy lives but to save them, was widely read in the ancient church, including by Ambrose and passed into the King James Version.

In the liturgy, the Revised Common Lectionary reads 9:28-36 (with 37-43) on the last Sunday after the Epiphany in Year C and 9:51-62 in the season after Pentecost. The Roman lectionary reads the transfiguration (9:28b-36) on the Second Sunday of Lent in Year C, the feeding (9:11b-17) on the solemnity of the Body and Blood of Christ in Year C, a reading chosen for its eucharistic overtones, and 9:18-24 and 9:51-62 on the twelfth and thirteenth Sundays in Ordinary Time.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from the manuscripts. In verse 10 the critical text says Jesus withdrew to a town called Bethsaida; some manuscripts read a deserted place, and the later Byzantine text combines the two, which the King James Version follows (‘into a desert place belonging to the city called Bethsaida’). In verse 23 the word daily (kath' hēmeran) is read by the oldest manuscripts and the Textus Receptus, but it is missing from many Byzantine manuscripts, perhaps by assimilation to Mark 8:34 and Matthew 16:24, which lack it. In verse 35 the papyri P45 and P75 and Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read ‘My Son, the Chosen One’ (ho eklelegmenos), while many later manuscripts read ‘My beloved Son’, matching Mark 9:7 and Matthew 17:5 and followed by the King James Version. The less familiar reading is almost certainly original, since scribes tended to harmonize the Gospels.

The largest difference is in verses 54-56. After James and John ask whether to call down fire, many later manuscripts and the Byzantine majority add ‘as Elijah also did’, which the earliest papyri (P45, P75) and Codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack. After Jesus rebukes them, some witnesses, among them Codex Bezae, add, ‘and He said, You do not know what kind of spirit you are of’; a still longer form, found in many later manuscripts and families and in the King James Version, continues, ‘for the Son of Man did not come to destroy people's lives but to save them’. The earliest witnesses have none of these words, and Bruce Metzger's Textual Commentary rates the shorter text of verse 54 as probable and of verses 55-56 as virtually certain. Modern versions print the short text and often give the additions in a footnote, which is why the BSB's verse 55 reads simply that Jesus turned and rebuked them. The additions agree with Jesus' teaching elsewhere (19:10) and circulated widely in the ancient church, but they were most likely explanatory expansions by scribes.

In verse 3 translations differ over whether the Twelve may take a staff: Luke and Matthew 10:10 forbid it, while Mark 6:8 allows one. The Gospel writers apply the same saying differently, and harmonizers have proposed that Mark permits the staff one already has while Matthew and Luke forbid acquiring another.

teach.big: Jesus is the Christ of God and the chosen Son whose glory leads through the cross, and to follow him is to deny oneself, take up the cross daily, and go where he goes without conditions.

outline.t: Jesus shares his authority with ordinary disciples and sends them dependent on God and on those who welcome them.
Curiosity about Jesus is not faith; Herod wants to see him but not to follow him.
Jesus welcomes the crowd and makes the disciples' meager resources enough, with more left over than they began with.
Confessing Jesus as the Christ is the beginning, and he at once defines his messiahship by the cross.
The disciple's life is shaped like his: self-denial, a daily cross, and the paradox that losing life for him is finding it.
The glory of the Son is revealed to strengthen those who must follow him to the cross; the Father's one command is to listen to him.
Down from the mountain the world's need is real and disciples fail, yet the greatness of God is shown, and Jesus again points to his betrayal.
Greatness in the kingdom is measured by welcoming the least, not by rank, and not by guarding our group's boundaries.
Jesus sets out resolutely for Jerusalem and refuses to answer rejection with vengeance.
Following Jesus admits no conditions: not comfort, not even the strongest duties, not a divided heart.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. Take up your cross is often reduced to enduring an ordinary burden, an illness or a difficult relative. In context it means accepting rejection and loss for Jesus' sake, as he accepted it; daily extends it to every day, but does not turn it into general hardship. The opposite error treats self-denial as self-hatred or as a call to accept abuse; Jesus calls disciples to lose their lives for his sake (verse 24), not to submit to others' cruelty.

The feeding is sometimes explained as a miracle of sharing, in which the crowd produced hidden food, a reading popularized in the nineteenth century. It does not fit Luke's account, which presents a sign of Jesus' power and provision. With the transfiguration, avoid mountaintop preaching that treats spiritual experience as the goal; Peter's wish to stay is gently set aside, and the voice directs attention to listening to Jesus. With verses 49-50, avoid using ‘whoever is not against you is for you’ to erase every doctrinal boundary; the point is that disciples must not claim a monopoly on Jesus' name. And with verses 51-56 and 57-62, do not turn Jesus' refusal of vengeance into indifference to evil or his demand into contempt for family: he honors parents elsewhere (18:20) and simply ranks the kingdom above even that honor.
teach.pastoral: The sayings about burying a father and saying goodbye to family (verses 59-62) will press on people who are grieving a parent, caring for aging parents, or estranged from family. Make clear that Jesus is not forbidding grief or care; he is naming the kingdom as the first loyalty that orders all others. The call to deny oneself will be heard differently by someone in an abusive relationship; teach that the cross Jesus calls us to carry is chosen for his sake, not suffering imposed by another person, and that seeking safety is not a failure of discipleship. The father's plea for his only son (verses 38-42) will reach parents of children with seizures, disabilities, or mental illness, and those who have asked the church for help and found it powerless, as he did with the disciples. Jesus' answer, bring your son here, invites honest lament and continued coming.

hard.q: What did Jesus mean when he said some standing there would not die before they saw the kingdom of God (verse 27)?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. If the saying refers to the final coming of the kingdom at the end of history, it seems not to have happened in the disciples' lifetime, and Jesus appears to have been mistaken. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) built his portrait of Jesus on this conclusion: Jesus expected the end of the world imminently and died disappointed. Bertrand Russell (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927) cited this saying, in its Matthean form, as evidence that Jesus was not as wise as Christians claim, since he expected his return within the lifetime of his hearers. Jewish and skeptical critics have often treated the unfulfilled expectation as one of the clearest marks of the historical Jesus.

Interpreters have offered several answers. Many from the early church onward, among them John Chrysostom in his homilies on Matthew, connect it with the transfiguration, which all three Synoptic Gospels place immediately after it: some of the disciples (Peter, James, and John) saw the kingdom's glory within days, and 2 Peter 1:16-18 treats the transfiguration as a witness to Christ's power and coming. Others point to the resurrection, ascension, and outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, when the kingdom came in power, as Luke describes in Acts. Others link it to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 as a visible act of judgment. Luke's wording is simpler than Mark's: where Mark 9:1 speaks of the kingdom come with power and Matthew 16:28 of the Son of Man coming in his kingdom, Luke says only that they will see the kingdom of God. Hans Conzelmann argued that Luke deliberately recast such sayings to address the delay of the end. Most Christian readers see these answers as overlapping rather than competing, since the transfiguration, the resurrection, and Pentecost are all glimpses of the same kingdom whose fullness is still to come. Readers who do not share that framework will judge whether the reinterpretations are faithful to Jesus or rescue him, and the question remains one of the central debates in historical Jesus research.

hard.q: Did Jesus really tell a man not to bury his father (verses 59-60)?
hard.a:
The objection comes from within Jewish law itself. Honoring father and mother is one of the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:12), and burial of the dead was among the weightiest duties of love; Tobit is praised for burying the dead at risk to himself (Tobit 1:17-19), and the Mishnah exempts a man whose dead lies before him even from reciting the Shema (m. Berakhot 3:1). Martin Hengel (1968) concluded that the saying is almost without parallel in Jewish or Greek antiquity in its offense against piety, and E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985) judged it the one place where Jesus clearly required a follower to break a commandment. Jewish readers have sometimes seen in it the kind of demand that set Jesus' movement apart from, and against, Jewish family obligation.

Responses fall into three groups. Some soften the setting: the father may still have been alive, so the man was postponing discipleship indefinitely; or, following Byron McCane (1990), the father had been buried and the son was waiting for the reburial of the bones a year later. Either way, Jesus is refusing an indefinite delay rather than forbidding a funeral. A second group, including Hengel and Sanders, holds that the saying means what it says and that its shock is the point: the kingdom's claim through Jesus outranks even the holiest duty, much as priests and Nazirites were forbidden to defile themselves even for close relatives (Leviticus 21:11, Numbers 6:6-7) and as Ezekiel was forbidden to mourn his wife as a sign (Ezekiel 24:15-18). A third reading focuses on the phrase the dead: those who are spiritually dead can handle such matters, while the one who is called must proclaim the kingdom of life. Readers across these positions agree that Jesus is not teaching contempt for parents; he affirms the command to honor them (18:20). What remains, however it is softened, is a claim of authority over the deepest human loyalties that only God could rightly make.

observe: What did the crowds say about who Jesus was, and what did Peter say?
